name: Restoration of Bahraini Citizenship

qualifying_event.description: The Bahraini Citizenship Act provides that citizenship may be restored to any person who has lost it -- whether through deception-based revocation, a qualifying criminal conviction, voluntary acquisition of a second nationality, unauthorized foreign military service, or conduct deemed to harm state security. This is a genuine restoration mechanism written into the statute itself, distinct from ordinary naturalisation or a Royal-Order discretionary grant. On 21 April 2019, King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa issued a royal order restoring citizenship to 551 individuals who had been stripped of Bahraini nationality, many following the 2011 unrest-related mass trials -- the single largest documented use of this provision, though only tier-3/4 press-sourced, not confirmed via any government announcement page found in this research.
qualifying_event.evidence_hint: Documentation of the prior revocation and the grounds under which it occurred.

requirements.blocker_text: Previously held and lost Bahraini citizenship through one of the statute's revocation mechanisms, and citizenship is restored at the discretion of the granting authority.

evidence_required.document: Documentation of prior citizenship and the circumstances of its loss

sources.title: GLOBALCIT (EUI academic citizenship-law observatory) -- English translation of the Bahraini Citizenship Act 1963, as amended: 'Citizenship of Bahrain may be restored to any person who has lost citizenship' -- a discretionary restoration provision distinct from ordinary naturalisation

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Bahrain). STATUS: DRAFT -- same tier-2 GLOBALCIT sourcing caveat as the other Bahraini citizenship files. MARQUEE HUMAN-RIGHTS-CONTEXT FINDING, DISCLOSED NOT ASSERTED AS DATASET FACT: Bahrain's revocation practice between roughly 2012 and 2019 -- hundreds of activists and dissidents denaturalized in the post-2011 unrest era -- drew sustained criticism from Human Rights Watch and ADHRB as being used punitively against political opponents, and this pattern is documented almost exclusively via tier-3/4 human-rights and press sources, not government sources (expected for a politically sensitive practice, but flagged so the dataset doesn't overstate its own sourcing confidence here). The 21 April 2019 mass restoration of citizenship to 551 individuals is the best-documented use of this provision but rests entirely on tier-3/4 international press (France24, Khaleej Times, VOA, Bloomberg-adjacent reporting) -- no tier-1 government announcement page was found. This route is modeled at the level of the general legal mechanism (the statute's restoration clause itself, tier-2 sourced), not the 2019 event specifically, since the event is not independently tier-1/2 confirmed. Selection_method is 'assessed' reflecting the same discretionary character as the rest of Bahrain's citizenship system.
